items.prompt: How did the leg posture of most dinosaurs differ from that of a modern lizard?

options.label: Their legs stood upright, straight under the body
options.feedback: Bones angled to the sides so the whole leg worked as a straight column beneath the hip, not held out and dragged around it.

options.label: Their legs sprawled out to the sides
options.feedback: That is the lizard's own posture — legs out sideways, belly low, a body swung side to side with every stride.

options.label: They had no legs at all, only flippers
options.feedback: Flippers belong to the plesiosaur and the ichthyosaur, ocean reptiles that lived alongside dinosaurs, not dinosaurs themselves.

options.label: Their legs were jointed only at the hip
options.feedback: A leg with a single joint could not bend to take a stride; the knee and ankle did as much of the work as the hip.

items.ok_line: A column of bone under the body, not a strut jutting from the side.
items.ko_line: Picture a lizard's belly dragging low, then picture a dog's legs straight beneath it.
items.exp_text: A lizard's hip socket points sideways, so its thigh bone juts outward and its stride swings the whole body left and right to reach forward. In most dinosaurs the hip socket instead opened downward, turning the thigh bone into a nearly straight column planted under the hip. Weight travelled straight down through bone rather than being carried on muscle holding a bent leg out sideways, letting a dinosaur cover ground with less effort at each step.

items.prompt: How could a long-necked dinosaur such as Brachiosaurus hold its neck out without the weight snapping it down?

options.label: The neck bones were filled with air, not solid
options.feedback: Branches of the lung pushed into pockets inside each neck bone, hollowing it from within and cutting its weight without cutting its strength.

options.label: The neck was mostly cartilage, which bends easily
options.feedback: Cartilage would sag under such a long reach; the neck was built of bone, just bone lightened from inside.

options.label: Powerful muscles alone carried the weight
options.feedback: Muscle strong enough to hold up a solid-boned neck that long would itself have added more weight than it saved.

options.label: The neck rested along the ground most of the time
options.feedback: A neck dragged on the ground could not reach the treetop foliage these animals fed on.

items.ok_line: A neck built light, bone by bone, the way a bird's wing is.
items.ko_line: Ask what was hollowed out, not what held it up.
items.exp_title: A neck hollowed from the inside
items.exp_text: Air sacs branching off the lungs pushed into pockets carved into each vertebra of the neck, so the bone that formed was riddled with air spaces rather than solid through and through. Thin walls of bone kept the strength of a column while cutting away most of what would otherwise have been dead weight. A neck built this way could be extended a long way from the shoulders without the muscles needed to lift a solid version.

items.prompt: How did duck-billed dinosaurs such as Edmontosaurus cope with wearing down their teeth on tough plants?

options.label: They swallowed stones to do the grinding instead
options.feedback: Stone-swallowing helped some plant-eating dinosaurs, but the duck-bills relied on their teeth themselves, not on stones in the gut.

options.label: Their teeth kept growing back as fast as they wore down
options.feedback: Rows of teeth waited beneath the working ones, packed edge to edge, and pushed up to replace each tooth as it wore away.

options.label: Their jaws stopped growing new teeth after hatching
options.feedback: The opposite is closer to the truth: replacement never stopped through the animal's life.

options.label: They avoided tough plants and ate only soft leaves
options.feedback: Wear on the fossil teeth themselves shows a diet gritty and fibrous enough to grind them down steadily.

items.ok_line: A conveyor belt of teeth, always ready with the next one.
items.ko_line: The wear on a duckbill's teeth was real; the question is what kept replacing them.
items.exp_title: Rows of teeth waiting in reserve
items.exp_text: A duck-billed dinosaur's jaw held many teeth packed into tight columns, with only the topmost tooth of each column actually chewing at any moment. Beneath it sat several more teeth, each partly grown, ready to move up and take its place the moment it wore through. Chewing tough, gritty plant matter all day wore teeth down quickly, and this stack of replacements kept a fresh grinding surface in use without the animal ever going without one.

items.prompt: How did an ankylosaur's tail club most likely work as a defence?

options.label: It sprayed a foul-smelling liquid at attackers
options.feedback: No dinosaur is known to have had a spray defence like this; that trick belongs to certain living insects and mammals.

options.label: It released a cloud of dust to hide the animal
options.feedback: The tail's mass was bone, not anything that could be released into the air.

options.label: It was purely decorative and had no defensive use
options.feedback: The stiffened tail vertebrae leading up to the club are built the way a handle is built for something meant to be swung, not simply displayed.

options.label: It was swung sideways to strike a predator's legs
options.feedback: Muscles and stiffened tail vertebrae let the animal whip the bony mass at the end of its tail into an attacker's legs or ankles hard enough to injure them.

items.ok_line: A bony hammer at the end of a stiffened handle.
items.ko_line: Look at what the last several tail vertebrae are fused into: a handle for something.
items.exp_title: A handle built to swing a weight
items.exp_text: The vertebrae partway down an ankylosaur's tail were fused into a stiff rod, and strong muscles anchored along that rod could whip the free end sideways. At the tip sat a mass of solid bone, heavy enough that a swing landing on a predator's leg could break it. A hunter that came in low to bite at the legs risked meeting that swing rather than a target that simply stood still.

items.prompt: Why were the bony plates down a Stegosaurus's back probably not useful as armour?

options.label: They were too thin and full of blood vessels to block a bite
options.feedback: Cut open, the plates show channels that once carried blood vessels through a fairly thin sheet of bone — better suited to controlling heat than stopping teeth.

options.label: They were located on the belly, not the back
options.feedback: The plates stood up in a row along the spine, in clear view, not underneath where a belly would need protecting.

options.label: They could be shed and regrown like antlers
options.feedback: The plates were fixed, permanent parts of the skeleton, not something dropped and regrown each year.

options.label: They were made of the same soft tissue as skin
options.feedback: The plates were bone, hard enough to fossilize on their own, not soft tissue.

items.ok_line: Riddled with blood vessels — a radiator, not a shield.
items.ko_line: Look at what runs through the inside of a plate once you cut one open.
items.exp_text: Slice through a fossil Stegosaurus plate and it is crossed with grooves that once carried blood vessels close to its surface, in a sheet of bone far too thin to have stopped a predator's teeth. That same thinness serves heat instead: blood running just under a broad flat surface sheds warmth quickly on a hot day, or gains it quickly turned toward the sun. A body regulates its temperature far faster through a wide, thin, blood-filled sheet like that than it ever could through a slab of solid armour.

items.prompt: Why were the teeth of a meat-eating dinosaur such as Allosaurus serrated along the edge, like a steak knife?

options.label: To help pull tough plant fibres apart
options.feedback: Serrations for shredding fibrous plants belong to some plant-eating dinosaurs; this shape of tooth belonged to a hunter, curved and blade-like, not flattened for grinding.

options.label: To make a rattling sound to frighten prey
options.feedback: A closed mouth makes no sound from its teeth; the serrations only do their work once the jaw is already biting.

options.label: To saw through flesh and tendon as the jaw bit down
options.feedback: Tiny saw-like ridges along the edge let the tooth cut cleanly through muscle and sinew instead of just squeezing them, the way a serrated knife slices where a smooth blade would slip.

options.label: To filter small animals out of water
options.feedback: Filtering teeth are long and comb-like, built to strain, not the short curved blades a hunting dinosaur carried.

items.ok_line: A row of tiny saw teeth on every big one.
items.ko_line: Think about what a serrated edge does differently from a smooth one, on a knife or on a tooth.
items.exp_title: A blade edged like a saw
items.exp_text: Under magnification, the curved edge of a theropod's tooth is lined with tiny saw-like points, each one angled the same way down the length of the tooth. A smooth blade pressed into meat tends to squeeze and slip past tough fibres, while a serrated edge catches on them and parts them cleanly as the jaw closes. The same saw-toothed edge ran the length of every tooth in the jaw, front to back, so each bite cut rather than just crushed.

items.prompt: Why did a two-legged, meat-eating dinosaur such as Tyrannosaurus carry its body roughly level, with a long stiff tail stretched out behind?

options.label: To use the tail as a whip against attackers
options.feedback: The tail's stiffness suits balance far better than a whip would; whipping needs a flexible tail lashing side to side, not one held rigid and straight.

options.label: To balance the weight of its head and body over its hips
options.feedback: With the hips as a pivot, a heavy tail out the back balanced a heavy head and body out the front, the way two children balance a see-saw.

options.label: Because its legs were too short to lift it upright
options.feedback: The legs were long and powerful, well able to lift the body clear off the ground; the tail's role was balance, not compensating for weak legs.

options.label: To store fat for lean seasons
options.feedback: A tail this muscular and boned would be a poor place to store fat compared with soft tissue elsewhere in the body.

items.ok_line: A see-saw with the hips as the pivot.
items.ko_line: Think of the hips as a fixed point with weight on both sides of it.
items.exp_title: Balanced over the hips like a see-saw
items.exp_text: Walking on two legs puts the hips at a single narrow point of support, and anything heavy hanging unbalanced to one side would topple the animal forward or backward. A massive skull and neck stuck out in front of the hips, so a long, muscular, stiffened tail stretched out an equal distance behind them, weight for weight. Held level this way, the body's centre of balance sat almost directly above the legs instead of pitching forward with every stride.

items.prompt: Since sauropods like Diplodocus had small, weak-looking heads on enormous bodies, how did they get enough nourishment from tough plants?

options.label: They chewed for hours before swallowing
options.feedback: Their small, simple teeth and jaws show little sign of the grinding chewing action needed to do this; the head was built for stripping leaves, not milling them.

options.label: They ate only the softest, most digestible plants
options.feedback: Fossil evidence of the plants available to them points to coarse, fibrous vegetation, not a diet chosen for softness.

options.label: They absorbed nutrients directly through the skin
options.feedback: No animal digests its food through the skin; nutrients from a meal are absorbed only after it has passed into the gut.

options.label: They swallowed leaves whole and let a huge gut do the work
options.feedback: Stripped straight off branches and swallowed with barely any chewing, plant matter travelled to an enormous gut where it sat long enough for it to be slowly broken down.

items.ok_line: A small head for stripping leaves, a vast gut for the rest of the job.
items.ko_line: If the mouth barely chewed, ask where the real breaking-down happened.
items.exp_title: A small mouth serving an enormous gut
items.exp_text: A sauropod's jaws and simple peg-like teeth were suited to stripping leaves from a branch in one motion, not to grinding them the way a flat-toothed grazer would. Almost unchewed, that plant matter travelled down into a gut large enough to hold it for a long stretch of time, where it was broken down instead by fermentation, aided by microbes living inside. Given enough time and enough volume inside that gut, even coarse, fibrous leaves eventually yielded up their nourishment.

items.prompt: How did a hard-shelled dinosaur egg let dinosaurs lay their eggs on dry land, away from water?

options.label: The shell was airtight, sealing the embryo inside completely
options.feedback: A fully sealed shell would suffocate the embryo inside; the shell instead needed to let air through, not keep all of it out.

options.label: The shell was soft and rubbery, like a turtle egg
options.feedback: Many dinosaur eggshells found are hard and brittle enough to fossilize on their own, not the leathery kind.

options.label: The shell was full of tiny pores that let air in and out
options.feedback: Countless microscopic pores ran through the hard shell, letting oxygen reach the embryo and waste gas escape, while holding the fluid around the embryo safely inside.

options.label: The eggs were laid directly into shallow water
options.feedback: Fossil nests are found on land, often shaped into mounds or scrapes, not laid into water.

items.ok_line: Sealed enough to hold water in, open enough to let air through.
items.ko_line: The shell had to do two opposite jobs at once: keep something in, and let something else through.
items.exp_title: A shell that breathes without leaking
items.exp_text: Earlier land animals like amphibians had to lay their soft eggs in or near water, since a naked egg dries out fast in open air. A hard, mineral eggshell solved that by sealing a private pool of fluid around the embryo, holding it safe from drying no matter how dry the surrounding ground was. That same shell was pierced through by pores too small to see, letting oxygen reach the embryo and carbon dioxide leave without ever letting the fluid inside escape.

items.prompt: How did the asteroid strike at the end of the Cretaceous period wipe out the non-bird dinosaurs even far from where it hit?

options.label: The blast wave circled the planet and flattened everything
options.feedback: A shockwave loses its force with distance; it could level forests near the impact but could not reach around the whole planet.

options.label: Dust and debris blocked sunlight, and the food chain collapsed
options.feedback: Material thrown high into the atmosphere spread worldwide and dimmed the sun for a long stretch of time, starving plants first and then everything that depended on them.

options.label: The ground shook so hard that every animal on Earth died at once
options.feedback: An earthquake's force fades with distance from its source, and nothing shakes the entire planet at the same moment.

options.label: Ash rained down and poisoned every water source
options.feedback: Ash fallout was real near the impact, but the extinction reached animals on every continent, far beyond where fallen ash could poison water directly.

items.ok_line: The sky itself was the weapon, everywhere at once.
items.ko_line: Whatever caused a worldwide extinction had to reach every continent, not just the impact site.
items.exp_title: A darkened sky, a broken food chain
items.exp_text: Rock and dust thrown high above the atmosphere by the impact spread on the wind until it wrapped the whole planet, and for a long stretch of time far less sunlight reached the ground than plants needed. Plants that could not draw enough light to grow died back or stopped producing food, and the plant-eating animals that depended on them starved not long after. Every meat-eater in turn lost the prey it depended on, so the collapse spread upward through the food chain long after the impact itself had passed.
